Nobody’s expecting Oliver Glasner to get the old heave-ho should Forest extend their miserable record tonight, but with the Tricky Trees currently above the relegation places only thanks to goal difference, the Austrian could do with three precious points and a little time and space. But they were hammered 4-1 at home by big rivals Leeds last weekend , their second Premier League defeat in a row and their third in four matches. The defence is in tatters, the midfield falls apart when Moisés Caicedo isn’t there, the style of play is yet to be determined, and the boss used to play for Liverpool. Another defeat would set the cat, if not among the pigeons, then a couple of paces behind them, quietly waiting for the most effective moment to pounce. Continue reading...

Business.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
Business.summary: Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances. Last Friday Levent Alpöge , a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis . Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog. Science.title: Breathing less oxygen tripled lifespan in mice with a deadly brain disorder
Science.summary: Oxygen is essential for life, but too much of it can become dangerously toxic, particularly in people with certain neurological and mitochondrial disorders. Scientists at Gladstone Institutes have discovered that defective proteins can disrupt the ability of mitochondria to consume oxygen, allowing harmful levels to accumulate in tissues. Remarkably, mice with a genetic disorder that causes motor neuron degeneration lived three times longer when they breathed air containing less oxygen.

Culture.title: DJ Tink, drop the beat! Peter Pan hits Club NVRLND for some noughties nostalgia
Culture.summary: The Vaults, London X Factor’s Diana Vickers leads this trip back to the 00s, as JM Barrie’s story is retooled as a night of pop bangers How about if Peter Pan, refusing to grow up, was a stunted man-boy lost in the what-ifs of his youth? He might be the promoter of a noughties club night, stuck in his glory days where everyone’s dressed like Girls Aloud meets the Vengaboys and the world hasn’t yet gone into meltdown. NVRLAND is that club, and this show – created by Steven Kunis and Jack Holden – is halfway between a jukebox musical and a cheesy disco, masterminded, surely, for the Christmas party crowd to down oversweet cocktails before oversharing with someone they barely know from the finance department. It’s basically pantomime for millennials/zillennials, with lots of audience participation from the dancefloor. And after a bit of warming up, it is great, giddy fun. Continue reading...
